summary: Defines a Trust Anchor Locator for the RPKI, which lets Relying Parties download the current trust anchor CA certificate from one or more locations and check that its key matches the one in the locator. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A small card that says where to download the root certificate and what fingerprint it should have.

questions: what is an rpki trust anchor locator
how does an rpki relying party use a tal
why does rpki prefer https over rsync
subtitle: A small file that tells RPKI software where to fetch a root certificate and which key to expect.

tldr.problem: RPKI software needs a root certificate to start from, but the resources listed in that certificate change over time, and redistributing the certificate each time would be a burden.
tldr.mechanism: A Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) lists one or more rsync or HTTPS URIs for the trust anchor certificate plus its base64 public key. The software downloads the certificate and checks that its key matches.
tldr.outcome: The TAL stays constant as long as the key and location do not change. RFC 8630 adds HTTPS URIs and comments to the format, and obsoletes RFC 7730.

today: RFC 8630 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 7730, the earlier TAL definition.

sections.title: What the TAL Is For
sections.content:
RFC 8630 defines the Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). It distributes Trust Anchor (TA) material using a mix of out-of-band and online means. Relying Parties (RPs) that verify RPKI signed objects SHOULD support the format so that makers of TA material and RPs interoperate.

The RFC does not invent a new format for the TA itself. A TA in the RPKI is a self-signed X.509 CA certificate. The TAL is only the data used to retrieve and verify it.
sections.plainLanguage: The TAL is a little note that tells your computer where to download the root certificate and how to recognise the right one.

sections.title: Why Not Just Distribute the Certificate
sections.content:
RPKI certificates carry extensions listing IP address and AS number delegations, called Internet Number Resources (INRs). The INR set of a TA is likely to change over time. If the usual PKI practice of securely distributing the TA were followed, that distribution would have to be repeated every time the set changed.

Distributing the TAL securely avoids this. The TAL stays constant as long as the TA's public key and its location do not change, so the selected data in the TA can change without redistributing the TA itself.

The RFC notes that the TAL is analogous to the TrustAnchorInfo structure of RFC 5914. The RPKI community adopted the TAL format first and prefers its simple ASCII encoding to the binary ASN.1 encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The root certificate's contents change often, but the card only names where to get it and the key to check. So the card does not need replacing.

sections.title: The TAL File Format
sections.content:
A TA URI is a URI used to retrieve a current TA certificate. It MUST be an rsync URI or an HTTPS URI. A TAL is an ordered sequence of four parts:

  1. an optional comment section: lines starting with the hash character, followed by human-readable UTF-8 text, each ending with a line break;
  2. a URI section of one or more ordered lines, each holding a TA URI;
  3. a line break;
  4. a subjectPublicKeyInfo in DER format, encoded in base64. Line breaks MAY be inserted into the base64 string to avoid long lines.

Line breaks can be CRLF or LF.
sections.plainLanguage: The card has a note on top, then one or more addresses, then a long scrambled-looking line that is the key.

sections.title: Rules for the TAL and the TA Certificate
sections.content:
Each TA URI MUST point at a single object, never a directory or collection. That object MUST be a self-signed CA certificate conforming to the RPKI certificate profile. Its INR extensions MUST hold a non-empty set of resources and MUST NOT use the inherit form. Its public key MUST equal the key in the TAL, and the key MUST stay stable when the certificate is reissued for INR changes or renewed.

The stable key encourages running the TA CA offline, with a subordinate CA certificate holding the same INRs issued for online use. That lets the CRL of the issuer revoke the subordinate certificate if the online key is suspected compromised.

The TA MUST be published at a stable URI, and a reissued certificate MUST be available at the same URI. A self-signed certificate has no CRL or manifest. To withdraw a TA, including for key rollover, the entity MUST remove the object from the location in the TAL. When a TAL lists several URIs, the same certificate MUST be at each. For resilience, the RFC recommends that their domain names resolve to distinct IP addresses at diverse publication points, covered by Route Origin Authorization objects signed by different CAs.
sections.plainLanguage: The note must point to exactly one file. The file must be the same everywhere it is listed, and the key on the card must match the key inside it.

sections.title: How a Relying Party Uses a TAL
sections.content:
An RP SHOULD do four things: retrieve the object at one of the TA URIs, confirm it is a current self-signed RPKI CA certificate that fits the profile, confirm that its public key matches the one in the TAL, and run any other local checks it wants before accepting the publisher as a TA.

It SHOULD repeat these steps for each TAL every time it resynchronizes its local repository cache, and before the cached copy expires.

With several URIs, the RP MAY apply its own preference rule: the TAL order, random choice, or a ranking by something like connection establishment delay. If a connection fails or the key does not match, the RP SHOULD try the next URI in its ranking.
sections.plainLanguage: Download the file from one address. If the key on the card does not match, try the next address on the list.

sections.title: Transport and Security
sections.content:
rsync provides neither transport security nor a way for the RP to validate the host, so HTTPS is RECOMMENDED as the preferred scheme. A man in the middle cannot forge a CA certificate that passes the validation steps, but can stop the RP from learning about an updated certificate. RPs MUST validate the TLS certificate and host name when fetching over HTTPS, and SHOULD log any validation problem.

The RFC recommends following RFC 7525 and RFC 6125 for HTTPS, supporting DNS-ID identifiers, and avoiding the wildcard character in repository server certificate names.

The security section warns that compromise of a TA private key lets others masquerade as the TA. The TAL does not list the covered resources, so the certificate issuer could claim to be authoritative for any resource. RPs should either trust the issuers highly or issue their own self-signed TA that constrains subordinate certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Fetching over the secure web is safer than fetching with rsync, which cannot prove who it is talking to. Only trust root keys you really trust.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 7730
sections.content: Compared with RFC 7730, the format adds two things: HTTPS URIs are allowed, and an optional comment section is allowed. The RFC notes that current RPs may not support the new format yet. It therefore recommends that a TA operator keep also publishing a TAL in the RFC 7730 format for a time, until they are satisfied that RP tooling has been updated.
sections.plainLanguage: The new card can use secure web addresses and can have a note at the top. Keep the old-style card around for a while too.
